# Price and yield metrics

Price per unit area, rent, yield, vacancy and liquidity, split prime vs
secondary. Sources in [citations.md](../citations.md).

## What this run can and cannot give you

**Delivered:** a dated FX rate with a source and a series identifier; usable
price levels for **two** countries with a genuine prime-vs-rural split; vacancy
*definitions* with their scope caveats; and a label on every price series saying
whether it is asking price, appraised value or recorded transaction.

**Not delivered, for any of the nine countries:** a gross rental yield, a
price-to-rent ratio, or a days-on-market figure. A search of the whole corpus for
yield and liquidity terms returned no substantive hit. **The central comparison
table the research question implies cannot be built from this evidence base.**

Six of the nine have no usable price or rent level at all.

## FX — delivered

**1 EUR = 1.1567 USD, 14 August 2026**, ECB euro foreign exchange reference rate,
series **EXR.D.USD.EUR.SP00.A** [52][53]. Two independent ECB pages give the same
value.

From the same table [52]: **HUF 362.58** and **MXN 19.6592** per EUR, giving
USD/HUF = 362.58 ÷ 1.1567 = **313.46** and USD/MXN = 19.6592 ÷ 1.1567 =
**16.996**.

The ECB's own caveat, which belongs alongside any converted figure: the rates are
"for information purposes only" and "using the rates for transaction purposes is
strongly discouraged" [52]. No Costa Rican colón or Panamanian balboa rate is
published in this table.

## The measured-area problem — why no $/ft² figure appears in this study

A price per square metre converts to a price per square foot only if the measured
area basis is known, and the bases differ by country and do not match US gross
living area.

**The corpus establishes no measured-area basis for any price series.** France's
*loi Carrez* is not mentioned in any fetched file; Spain's *superficie útil* vs
*construida* is not mentioned; Italy's OMI methodology says only "per unità di
superficie in euro al mq" without defining the surface.

The single exception is not a price at all: France's statutory letting-fee
ceilings are expressed "par m² de **surface habitable**" [13] — which confirms
that at least three distinct legal area definitions coexist in French practice,
without telling us which one the notarial price series uses.

**Consequence.** Converting €6,120/m² to about $658/ft² is arithmetically
straightforward — 6,120 × 1.1567 = $7,079/m², ÷ 10.7639 = $658/ft² — and this
document declines to publish it as a US-comparable number. The user's baseline is
US cost per square foot, and a converted European figure on an unknown area basis
is not the same quantity. Flagging this rather than converting is the honest
answer to the brief's own instruction to qualify any measure.

## Price levels

### Hungary — the strongest data, and the prime-vs-rural split falls straight out

KSH STADAT table 18.1.2.8, average price of one **used** dwelling, 2025, updated
31 July 2026 [54]:

| Segment | Million HUF | ≈ USD at 313.46 HUF/USD |
|---|---|---|
| Budapest | **67.8** | **$216,300** |
| County seats | 43.2 | $137,800 |
| Towns | 36.2 | $115,500 |
| **Villages (national)** | **23.6** | **$75,300** |
| National, all | 41.6 | $132,700 |
| North Great Plain villages | **10.9** | **$34,800** |

New dwellings: Budapest 93.0 M HUF (≈$296,700), national 81.3 M HUF.

**Prime-to-rural ratio: 67.8 ÷ 23.6 = 2.87×**, or **6.22×** against the cheapest
regional village segment. This is the Hungarian analogue of the Paris-versus-rural
contrast the brief asked about.

Series type: **recorded transaction**, sourced from the NAV duty-office database
of sale contracts — but note KSH's own caveat that the aggregates are indicative
because there is limited scope to verify the data to statistical standards, and
that the scope is **transactions between private individuals only** [55]. Cells
with too few transactions are suppressed.

### Mexico — appraisal-based, on a restricted population

SHF index, H1 2025 [57]: national **average $1,862,524 MXN**, **median $1,200,000
MXN**, up 8.7% year on year. At 16.996 MXN/USD that is roughly $109,600 average
and $70,600 median.

Series type: **appraised value on mortgage-financed purchases only**. Cash
purchases are excluded — and cash purchases are disproportionately the foreign
buyer in coastal and resort markets, which is exactly the population this study
cares about. The index measures a segment the target investor may not be in.

### France — one region-level figure, and the Paris split fails

Chambre des Notaires de Paris, prices to end May 2026 [56]: **Île-de-France
existing apartments 6,120 €/m²**; existing houses €318,000. Standardised on the
Notaires-INSEE index method over the trailing three months of transactions, which
makes it deed-based rather than asking-price.

But this is **Île-de-France, not Paris**. The city-of-Paris page fetched with no
price data, the national notaires page returned chart titles whose values are
images, and **no rural French price figure exists anywhere in the corpus**. The
user's explicit Paris-versus-countryside requirement is therefore **not met for
France** — the one country where they named it.

No French rent level was retrieved either.

### Spain, Italy, Portugal, Greece, Costa Rica, Panama — no price or rent level

- **Spain**: the MIVAU *valor tasado* series and the ministry statistics index
  both returned HTTP 403 [69]; the statistical bulletin page fetched as a bare
  table of contents, including the municipal breakdown for towns over 25,000
  inhabitants that would have given the prime-vs-secondary split; the INE rent
  index page returned an unexecuted query shell.
- **Italy**: the OMI database is the right source and its methodology is
  documented — semi-annual min/max ranges per zone, **for both sale and rental
  values**, which is the only route in this study to a same-basis gross yield —
  but the query interface was never executed and **zero quotations were
  retrieved**. OMI's own caveat is that the quotations "non possono intendersi
  sostitutive della stima puntuale" and give "indicazioni di valore di larga
  massima": a broad-brush band, neither an appraisal nor a transaction record.
- **Portugal**: the INE local house-price statistics URL failed with an encoding
  error in the retrieval tooling, not at the source [70].
- **Greece**: both Bank of Greece property price pages returned HTTP 403 [64].
- **Costa Rica and Panama**: no price, rent or vacancy figure of any kind.

## Vacancy — definitions, not usable rates

The only vacancy source is the OECD Affordable Housing Database, indicator HM1.1,
updated 15 April 2024 [58]. Its definition, verbatim:

> "Vacant dwellings are defined as dwellings that are not occupied, and are not
> seasonal or holiday homes or dwellings meant for seasonal use. Nevertheless,
> some national statistics for unoccupied dwellings include secondary and/or
> holiday homes."

What it gives is ranges, not per-country point values: Spain and Portugal above
**12%** vacant excluding seasonal homes and above **23%** including them; and in
Portugal, Spain, France, Austria and Denmark, seasonal and holiday homes are **at
least 40% of all unoccupied dwellings**. Reference year 2022, except Portugal,
Slovenia and Spain at 2021.

**This is a census unoccupancy count, not a rental-market vacancy rate**, and the
OECD says so — most of the data are census-derived, national definitions differ,
and some countries count dwellings empty because the occupant is in prison or
care, or because the property needs major repair. Converting it into a
rental-vacancy assumption would inflate apparent letting risk precisely in the
second-home-heavy coastal regions this investor is considering.

Of the nine, only Spain, Portugal and France appear at all. **Italy, Greece,
Hungary, Mexico, Costa Rica and Panama have no vacancy figure.** Costa Rica
appears only for a different indicator: the lowest dwellings per thousand
inhabitants in the OECD set, at **310** against an OECD average of 468.

**Every yield figure in this study would therefore assume full occupancy.** Since
no yield figure survived anyway, the point is moot here — but it must not be
forgotten if yields are added later.

## The EU-wide relatives — indices, not levels

Eurostat, *Housing in Europe 2025*, text finalised late November 2025 [59]:

- **House prices 2010→2024: EU +53%.** Rose in every EU country **except Italy
  and Cyprus**. Largest rise **Hungary +231%**.
- **Rents 2010→2024: EU +25%.** Rose everywhere **except Greece, −16%**. Hungary
  +107%.
- **Inflation over the same period: EU +39%**, Hungary 86%, Greece 20%.

Two derived observations, computed from Eurostat's own figures rather than stated
by Eurostat: Hungarian nominal prices tripled against 86% inflation while
Hungarian rents rose only 107% — so **rents barely outpaced inflation while prices
rose sharply in real terms, which mechanically compresses gross yield**. And
Italian nominal prices were flat to down against 39% EU inflation, a real-terms
decline.

Housing cost overburden 2024 [59]: Greece **29% in cities and 28% in rural
areas**, the EU's highest, against an EU city rate of about 10% and rural 6%.

The Eurostat house price index is a **transaction-price index**, but it is an
index of change and cannot produce a level, a €/m² or a $/ft².

## Gaps

- Gross yield, price-to-rent, days on market: **all nine countries**.
- Price or rent level: **six of nine**.
- Measured-area basis: **all nine**, which blocks every m²→ft² conversion.
- Rental-market vacancy rate as distinct from census unoccupancy: **all nine**.
- The Paris-versus-rural split the user specifically asked for: **not met**.
- FX for Costa Rica and Panama: the ECB table does not cover CRC, and Panama's
  balboa is not quoted there.
